303	### Criterion 3: Establish Ground Truths
304	
305	Scores the **Ground Truths list** — a numbered list of verified facts with stable GT-IDs,
306	source citations, and a provenance label, with unverified and delegate-reported entries marked
307	with the `GT-N?` suffix — in the Ground Truths section (output section 3).
308	
309	**Provenance check (apply before banding).** A citation being present is not verification. For
310	each unsuffixed ground truth, ask whether the analysis read the asserted figure in the cited
311	source — `read-at-source` — or merely received it from a sub-agent, search result, or summary
312	without opening the citation (`reported-by-delegate`, which requires the `?`). Score against
313	what the analysis did, not against how well-formed the citation looks.
314	
315	- **Rigorous** — every GT-item carries a stable identifier (GT-1, GT-2, etc.) that matches
316	  the identifiers referenced in the Derivation Chains section; every verified GT has a source
317	  citation that is more specific than "common knowledge" or "known fact"; every GT carries a
318	  provenance label; every unverified or delegate-reported GT is marked with the `?` suffix;
319	  the `?`-marked GTs are **enumerated by ID** and that enumeration matches the suffixed entries
320	  in the Ground Truths list when checked against it; every unsuffixed GT feeding a
321	  HIGH-confidence chain names its read-at-source location; no assumption that was discarded in
322	  Phase 2 (Verdict: Discard) appears in this list. Every unsuffixed GT whose cited source is
323	  reachable feeds at least one HIGH-confidence chain EXCEPT: the Phase 3 failure record names
324	  the source as unreachable, in which case the GT may feed only MEDIUM or LOW chains, evidenced
325	  by that record naming which source and why unreachable.
326	
327	  **Check the enumeration, do not quote it.** Quoting the analysis's own provenance summary as
328	  the satisfying span does not discharge this criterion — that verifies a summary was written,
329	  not that it is correct. Read the Ground Truths list, collect the IDs actually carrying `?`,
330	  and compare against the enumeration. Cite the comparison as the satisfying span (*"enumerated
331	  GT-2, GT-5, GT-9, GT-14; list carries `?` on exactly those four"*). Where a stated count and
332	  its enumeration disagree, the enumeration governs and the mismatched count is itself a defect.
333	
334	  **Reachability is decided by the Phase 3 record, not re-decided here.** A source is reachable
335	  when the Phase 3 verification step opened it, and unreachable when the Phase 3 failure record
336	  names it with a specific reason; the analyst reads the record and does not re-argue
337	  reachability per ground truth. This requirement is not satisfied by a ground truth that feeds
338	  no chain at all — a GT no derivation chain consumes is already a Criterion 4 defect, and the
339	  requirement presupposes at least one load-bearing chain consumes the GT. A single unsuffixed
340	  GT whose reachable source feeds only MEDIUM or LOW chains bands this criterion Sound; the same
341	  shortfall across multiple GTs bands it Hand-wavy.

343	- **Sound** — GT-IDs are present and stable, but one or more verified GTs cite "common
344	  knowledge," "known fact," or no source at all; OR provenance labels are missing though the
345	  `?` suffixes themselves are correctly applied; OR one unread GT (unverified or
346	  delegate-reported) is used without the `?` suffix **and it feeds only MEDIUM or LOW
347	  confidence chains**; OR the `?`-marked GTs are summarized by a bare count rather than
348	  enumerated, though the suffixes in the list are themselves correct.

350	  An enumeration that **disagrees with the list** does not band here — it bands **Hand-wavy**.
351	  A count that merely accompanies a correct enumeration and disagrees with it is a defect but
352	  bands Sound, since the enumeration governs and remains checkable.

354	- **Hand-wavy** — GT-IDs are present but they are not stable (the same ID is used for

356	  OR the list includes an assumption that was assigned a Discard verdict in Phase 2; OR

358	  disagrees with the Ground Truths list** — an enumeration that omits a suffixed GT understates
359	  the analysis's unverified inputs in the direction that flatters it, and unlike a bare count it
360	  was checkable, so a mismatch is a stronger failure than never enumerating at all; OR **any
361	  unsuffixed GT feeds a HIGH-confidence chain without naming a read-at-source location** — a
362	  HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on a figure nobody read is the failure this criterion
363	  exists to catch, and a single instance is enough to land here.

365	  **Fix — acquire before you downgrade.** Branch one, preferred: acquire the evidence — open
366	  the cited source, per the Phase 3 verification step, and let the read move the provenance
367	  label. Branch two: downgrade the confidence — carry the `?` and drop the chain from HIGH,
368	  taken only when the source cannot be opened or opens without containing the asserted figure or wording. The preference, explicitly: acquisition is preferred when the source is reachable, because a gate whose only available Fix weakens the output resolves every failure toward less claim rather than more evidence. The unreachable case is not a free pass — the downgrade branch still requires the Phase 3 failure record, which source and why unreachable, or `citation does not support the claim`, so a reader can tell a downgrade from a skipped attempt.
369	
370	- **Absent** — no GT-IDs are assigned to any fact in the Ground Truths section; OR the Ground
371	  Truths section lists claims without distinguishing verified from unverified (no `?` suffix
372	  appears anywhere, no citations appear anywhere, and the list is undifferentiated); OR the
373	  section is absent or empty.

375	### Criterion 4: Reason Upward
376	
377	Scores **both** the **Derivation Chains** (output section 4) — one chain per conclusion,
378	formatted as `GT-N + GT-M → [intermediate claim] → [conclusion]` with at least one
379	intermediate step — **and** the **Abandoned Reasoning** section (output section 5).
380	Both sections are in scope for this criterion. Quoted span: where the band is determined by chain form or chain dependency, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's chain-form table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Derivation Chains prose directly. Folds in:
381	dead-end honesty, the no-analogies-as-direct-evidence ban (D-07), escape-valve policing for Abandoned
382	Reasoning (D-03), and hop validity and arithmetic. The one-line form is the degenerate case, used only when the whole chain fits on one physical line; a chain that does not fit uses the head-plus-arrow-led form, and a hop is split rather than continued on a second line.
383	
384	- **Rigorous** — every conclusion stated anywhere in the document (in section 4 or section 6)
385	  has exactly one derivation chain in section 4; each chain names the inputs it consumes — ground truths, upstream conclusions, or both — in the prescribed head form (`GT-1? ([brief fact label]) + C2 ([brief fact label])`),
386	  contains at least one intermediate claim (a claim that cannot be stated from any single named input alone), and reaches a conclusion; each chain is rendered in the prescribed
387	  arrow-led form. A hop occupies exactly one physical line. Every line after the head begins with `→` and carries exactly one complete hop; a hop is never broken across physical lines. The head line lists the inputs the chain consumes: each is a `GT-N` identifier (`GT-N?` when the ground truth is unverified) or a `Cn` identifier, optionally followed by a parenthesized gloss, joined to the next by `+`. The first `→` closes the head. An input carrying unparenthesized prose — `C2's threshold` — is not an identifier and does not parse; write `C2 (threshold)` in every position. The mechanical form check detects that violation only when the prose input is the last one before the first `→`; in an earlier position the check matches the well-formed remainder and scores the head conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The head grammar governs the head line only. A hop is prose: `C2's saving` is fine after the first `→`, and is not an input reference. One exception: a hop must not begin with a `GT-N` identifier, which the form check reads as the head of a new chain and which therefore ends this one — write `→ the duty cycle stated in GT-4 is the binding term`, not `→ GT-4's stated duty cycle is the binding term`. The form check detects that violation only while fewer than two hops precede it; in a later position the check matches the preceding hops and scores the chain conforming, so the rule binds in positions the check does not reach. The mechanical form check additionally rejects a chain whose head or first hop closes its own sentence before the next `→`: it reads the following arrow-led line as a new statement and ends the chain there, so a chain satisfying every rule above is scored malformed for that reason alone. The check reaches only that position — a hop that closes its own sentence from the second hop onward does not change the verdict — which is why intermediate hops carry no terminal punctuation in this project's worked examples. Hops rendered as an ordered list do not satisfy the prescribed form; the Abandoned Reasoning
388	  section either documents
389	  at least one dead end using the What-was-tried / Why-abandoned / What-it-ruled-out structure,
390	  OR uses the honest-depth escape valve with a reason that is specific to this analysis's
391	  problem and appears in no other analysis without alteration; no analogy
392	  is used as direct evidence (any reference to how others solved a similar problem is grounded
393	  in a named GT about their situation, not offered as standalone justification);
394	  each chain step that introduces an assumption not already in the Assumptions Table
395	  declares that assumption inline using `[Assumes: X]` appended to the step text —
396	  a reviewer applies this check by scanning each chain step for the `[Assumes:` token;
397	  and every hop the endpoint depends on follows from the line above it by deduction, by
398	  arithmetic that recomputes when redone independently of the chain text, or by a regularity
399	  cited to an unsuffixed ground truth — the test `output-template.md` states for the HIGH
400	  band under "Confidence levels, defined", shared here rather than restated. A hop that
401	  follows once the `[Assumes: X]` premise declared on that hop is granted counts as following
402	  for this criterion — declaring the premise takes the hop out of this limb by design, and
403	  whether that premise is priced is Criterion 5's Inference axis. An undeclared premise is not
404	  treated that way: a hop the endpoint depends on whose only gap is an undeclared premise is a
405	  non-sequitur under Hand-wavy below, and the `[Assumes: X]` limb above covers undeclared
406	  premises on hops the endpoint does not depend on; a hop citing
407	  a regularity to a `GT-N?` ground truth is an Inputs-axis matter Criterion 3/5 scores, not a
408	  failure to follow.
409	
410	- **Sound** — chains exist for all conclusions, but one or more chains lack a genuine
411	  intermediate step (the chain goes directly from its head inputs to conclusion, or the stated
412	  intermediate is a restatement of one of its named inputs rather than a new inference); OR
413	  a conclusion has more than one derivation chain — redundant restatement rather than a
414	  missing chain — where the prescribed form is exactly one chain per conclusion; OR
415	  one dead end in Abandoned Reasoning is described with a vague abandonment reason
416	  ("seemed unlikely," "ran out of time") rather than the specific structural reason
417	  (assumption false, contradicts a GT, circular, intermediate could not be established); OR
418	  one or more chains render their hops as an ordered list (`1.`, `2.`, `3.`) instead of the
419	  prescribed arrow-led hop form, OR break a single hop across physical lines rather than
420	  splitting it into two hops, which splits one chain into disconnected
421	  fragments even where every hop is individually sound; OR a hop fails to follow, or its
422	  arithmetic does not recompute, where the endpoint does not depend on that hop; OR a hop the
423	  endpoint depends on carries an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged — the
424	  only case of a hop the endpoint depends on that this band admits, and it covers arithmetic
425	  only: a hop the endpoint depends on that does not follow by deduction or cited regularity is
426	  Hand-wavy, whatever the grader judges its effect on the endpoint — **this clause is why the criterion
427	  cannot be scored on reasoning quality alone.** A chain that names its inputs, carries a
428	  genuine intermediate and reaches a conclusion satisfies every other Rigorous requirement
429	  while still failing the prescribed form; scoring only the semantics is what lets a
430	  Rigorous verdict coexist with a section of malformed chains.
431	
432	- **Hand-wavy** — some conclusions lack derivation chains; OR chains reference GT-IDs that
433	  do not appear in the Ground Truths section; OR an analogy is used as direct evidence
434	  ("others have solved it this way," "industry standard is X") without grounding in a named
435	  GT about that other situation; OR the Abandoned Reasoning section uses the honest-depth
436	  escape valve with a reason that is generic and would apply equally to any analysis (e.g.,
437	  "no dead ends were encountered," "all reasoning paths worked"); OR a hop the endpoint
438	  depends on does not follow by deduction or cited regularity (a non-sequitur) — including
439	  a hop whose only gap is an undeclared premise — or an arithmetic error changes the endpoint; an arithmetic error that leaves the endpoint unchanged
440	  is the Sound clause above, not this one — **this clause is why the criterion cannot be scored
441	  on form alone either.** A chain can name
442	  its inputs, carry a genuine intermediate, render every hop in the prescribed form and reach
443	  a conclusion while a hop the endpoint depends on does not follow.
444	
445	- **Absent** — no derivation chains exist in the document; OR the Derivation Chains section
446	  is absent or empty; OR conclusions appear in section 6 with no corresponding chains in
447	  section 4 — the core question's answer cannot be traced to any named ground truth.

449	### Criterion 5: Validate
450	
451	Scores the **signed-off analysis** — the complete output with all conclusions traced and weak
452	links resolved or explicitly flagged with confidence caveats — across all six output sections,
453	focusing on the confidence caveats attached to the Derivation Chains (output section 4).
454	
455	- **Rigorous** — every derivation chain's weakest link is named; every MEDIUM or LOW confidence
456	  caveat, on a chain or on the Conclusion section, explains only its own rating: it names each
457	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, with the verification that would remove that input as a
458	  cause of the downgrade, and each Cn its head cites — or, for the Conclusion section, each
459	  contributing chain — that is rated below HIGH, and it need not re-explain a named Cn, whose
460	  own caveat carries its explanation; and for each downgrade cause belonging to the chain or
461	  Conclusion itself, such as a weak inference step or an absent-fails derivation, it states
462	  what would remove it as a cause of the downgrade or a stated reason no verification path
463	  exists, that reason being either, for an absent-fails derivation, the absent-fails EXCEPT
464	  clause below, the only clause that can stand in for a verification path, or an explicit
465	  account of why no available evidence settles that cause;
466	  the overall Conclusion section's confidence rating (HIGH / MEDIUM / LOW) matches the weakest
467	  chain that contributes to it, counting only chains not covered by an EXCEPT clause stated in
468	  this same descriptor; no chain that consumes a GT-N? input is rated HIGH confidence; every
469	  chain is rated no higher than the lowest-rated chain its head cites, a ceiling that holds
470	  even when a cited chain is rated MEDIUM under an EXCEPT clause below.
471	  Every rating is calibrated: each chain carries the band its inputs, hops and rivals
472	  license under the three-axis definition in `output-template.md` — no chain rated above
473	  what those axes permit, and none rated below it. A Conclusion claim supported by
474	  at least one HIGH-confidence chain may be presented at HIGH; a claim with no such
475	  chain is presented at the band its weakest contributing chain licenses, and presenting
476	  it so is Rigorous rather than a shortfall. Under-rating is a defect of the same kind
477	  as over-rating, and this criterion scores calibration, not altitude. EXCEPT: a chain is explicitly marked speculative — for
478	  example `[Speculative]` — and the analysis states, in the same place, that the claim it
479	  supports is not load-bearing and is offered for exploration only; that mark plus that
480	  statement is the satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM, though its confidence
481	  line still gives each of its own downgrade causes what would remove it or an explicit account
482	  of why no available evidence settles it, because the mark is not a no-path reason; a
483	  speculative chain cited on another chain's head is load-bearing and no longer satisfies this
484	  EXCEPT clause, so a speculative chain with no verification path is not cited on another
485	  chain's head and instead stays speculative or moves to Abandoned Reasoning (output section 5).
486	  EXCEPT: a chain is
487	  an absent-fails derivation — of the form "if [assumption] were true we could conclude X;
488	  [assumption] is false; therefore X does not follow" — whose named false assumption is the
489	  satisfying evidence, and the chain may remain MEDIUM because it establishes what does not
490	  follow rather than what does.
491	
492	  The adversarial pass Phase 5 prescribes has run and its record is complete: each computed
493	  figure's recompute, the sensitivity ground truth and whether it is `?`-marked, the rival and
494	  where it is ruled out or carried live, a premise stated in the past tense, an unfiltered
495	  cause list written before any grouping, clusters each naming the chain ids or ground-truth
496	  ids the weakness bears on, per cluster a named plan change or an explicitly accepted risk
497	  with a named mitigation, and the falsification condition — each part present or carrying its
498	  step's not-applicable line. Each structural weakness the pass
499	  returned has landed somewhere a reader can find it — as a named weak link on a chain, or as
500	  an explicit confidence caveat on the conclusion it threatens. An analysis whose conclusion is
501	  neither a plan nor a claim satisfies the Premise, Causes, Clusters and Disposition parts by
502	  carrying the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line with its reason named — that
503	  line is the adversarial-technique step's own not-applicable line, not a waiver of the whole
504	  record, so the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts each still carry their
505	  content or their own step's not-applicable line; an analysis that does carry a plan or a claim
506	  cannot satisfy the technique step that way, and the reason given is what makes the two cases
507	  distinguishable.
508	
509	  **A conclusion without a HIGH chain is not a shortfall.** A conclusion resting on no
510	  HIGH-confidence chain, uncovered by either EXCEPT clause above, is Rigorous on this
511	  criterion when every band it rests on is the band that chain's axes license and the
512	  Conclusion's own rating equals its weakest contributing chain's. A MEDIUM or LOW overall
513	  Conclusion rating remains a legitimate, honestly-caveated analysis — `output-template.md`
514	  permits it and this criterion now scores it Rigorous when it is calibrated. What bands
515	  this criterion below Rigorous is a band that does not match its axes in either direction,
516	  never a band that is merely low, and a verdict block reporting Rigorous alongside a
517	  MEDIUM overall rating is the expected shape of an honest analysis rather than a
518	  contradiction. An exception is claimed, not assumed: an analysis relying on one of the
519	  two EXCEPT clauses above names it in the Criterion 5 verdict block and cites the evidence
520	  that clause requires; an unclaimed exception is not applied on the analysis's behalf.
521	
522	- **Sound** — confidence ratings exist on chains, but a MEDIUM or LOW confidence line omits a
523	  GT-N? input it rests on directly, or a Cn its head cites (or, on the Conclusion section, a
524	  contributing chain) that is rated below HIGH, or a downgrade cause belonging to its own chain
525	  or Conclusion — including a MEDIUM or LOW rating that no named GT-N? input or Cn accounts for
526	  and whose line names no cause of its own; OR a confidence line names a GT-N? input without the
527	  verification that would remove it as a cause of the downgrade; OR a confidence line gives a
528	  downgrade cause belonging to its own chain or Conclusion with neither what would remove it as
529	  a cause of the downgrade nor a permitted no-path reason — for an absent-fails derivation, the
530	  absent-fails EXCEPT clause, or an explicit account of why no available evidence settles that
531	  cause — including a line whose only account of such a cause is the speculative EXCEPT clause
532	  or any clause other than the absent-fails one; OR a chain's head cites a chain marked
533	  speculative that has no verification path; OR a chain is rated HIGH confidence while consuming
534	  a GT-N? input (the rating does not match the unverified-input rule); OR a chain is rated above
535	  the lowest-rated chain its head cites; OR a single chain's band does not match what its
536	  three axes license, in either direction — a chain rated HIGH whose head carries a `?` or
537	  whose hops rest on a stated `[Assumes: A-N]` premise, or a chain meeting all three axes
538	  rated MEDIUM — while every other chain in the analysis is correctly banded; OR an
539	  adversarial pass record, or the `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line, is present
540	  but one or more of the Recompute, Sensitivity, Rival and Falsification parts is absent and
541	  carries no not-applicable line of its own — a step silently omitted from a pass that otherwise
542	  ran.
543	
544	- **Hand-wavy** — confidence ratings appear on the overall Conclusion section but are absent
545	  from individual derivation chains; OR weak links are described in general terms ("some
546	  assumptions remain uncertain") without naming the specific chain step or GT-N? input that
547	  caused the concern; OR an adversarial pass record is present but no cluster carries a
548	  disposition — neither a named plan change nor an explicitly accepted risk with a named
549	  mitigation — so the pass named structural weaknesses and acted on none of them; OR the record
550	  states its clusters without the cause list they were drawn from, which is the generic risk
551	  list the pass exists to replace rather than a pass that produced one; OR two or more
552	  chains carry bands their axes do not license, so the miscalibration is a pattern rather
553	  than an isolated entry; OR every chain in the analysis carries the same band and no
554	  confidence line names which axis produced it, which is a default setting rather than a
555	  rating.
556	
557	- **Absent** — no confidence ratings appear anywhere in the derivation chains; OR GT-N? inputs
558	  are used in load-bearing chains without any confidence caveat anywhere in the document; OR
559	  — covering the case the first two clauses miss — confidence ratings exist but no weak-link
560	  identification or chain inspection was performed at all, so there is no evidence that
561	  Phase 5's stress-test operation was executed; OR neither an adversarial pass record nor an
562	  `adversarial pass not applicable — [reason]` line appears anywhere in the response, so there
563	  is no evidence that Phase 5's adversarial pass was executed at all. These two clauses are
564	  separate readings: a weakest-link paragraph written by the same reasoning that built the
565	  chains satisfies the first and not the second, and an analysis scoring above Absent on the
566	  strength of that paragraph alone is what this clause exists to catch.
567	
568	### Criterion 6: Conclusion-to-Ground-Truth Traceability
569	
570	Scores the relationship between the **Conclusion section** (section 6) claims and the
571	**Derivation Chains** (section 4) that produced them — a cross-section structural property
572	of the signed-off analysis as a whole. Quoted span: where the band is determined by whether a section-6 claim traces to a named section-4 chain, it must be drawn from the self-audit scan's claim-inventory table row or rows that determine the band, not from the Conclusion prose directly. Where the band is determined by the Key Insight being a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a non-obvious finding — a semantic property the claim-inventory table carries no column for — quote the analysis text directly.
573	
574	- **Rigorous** — every claim in the Conclusion section (recommended approach, key insight,
575	  trade-offs acknowledged) traces to a specific named derivation chain in section 4; the
576	  Conclusion section introduces no new claims that did not appear in section 4; the Key
577	  Insight names a non-obvious finding — a result that reasoning by analogy or convention
578	  does not reach — rather than restating the recommended approach.
579	
580	- **Sound** — most Conclusion claims trace to chains in section 4, but one claim is introduced
581	  for the first time in the Conclusion section (new reasoning not present in any derivation
582	  chain); OR the Key Insight is a restatement of the recommended approach rather than a
583	  non-obvious finding.
584	
585	- **Hand-wavy** — the Conclusion section contains claims that contradict or are inconsistent
586	  with the derivation chains in section 4; OR multiple new claims appear in the Conclusion
587	  section that are not present in any derivation chain.
588	
589	- **Absent** — the Conclusion section contains claims with no corresponding derivation chain
590	  anywhere in section 4; OR the Conclusion section is absent or empty; OR every item in the
591	  Conclusion is new reasoning not established by any derivation chain — the Conclusion section
592	  has been used to introduce the analysis's conclusions rather than to synthesize them.
593	
594	The extraction and caveat rules the bands above are scored against are stated here verbatim so the grading instrument carries them, not just the surface it grades.
595	
596	A Conclusion-section claim is a bold lead-in whose colon closes the bold span, or a numbered or bulleted list item, and the four lead-ins this template prescribes — `**Recommended approach:**`, `**Key insight:**`, `**Trade-offs acknowledged:**` and `**Confidence:**` — are always claims and each must cite a chain; the `**Confidence:**` line discharges that obligation through the chains D-07 already requires it to name, and a HIGH line whose justification prose names no chain is the one position where this rule and the extractor can disagree, so name the chain there too; nothing inside a fenced block is ever a claim whatever its shape, a near-paraphrase restatement or direct entailment of an already-cited claim earlier in the same section is not a second claim, and prose carrying neither a bold colon lead-in nor a list marker is not a claim at all. Enumerate by this rule, not by recollection — the rule is the contract and the extractor is a partial instrument for it.
597	
598	A caveat qualifying an existing Conclusion-section claim either names the chain it qualifies inline or carries the marker `no chain — flagged assumption only` (em dash, lower case, no trailing punctuation inside the marker), and a marked caveat still scores untraced: the marker discloses the gap, it does not discharge the claim, because it is honest labelling rather than a citation and the extractor is deliberately not taught to recognise it. A caveat doing neither is cut, not softened.
599	
600	---
601	
602	## Usage Note
603	
604	Score every criterion. Produce one verdict block per criterion, using the prescribed format
605	from the Verdict Block Format section above. The analysis must clear the gate (no criterion
606	at Absent) and the hand-wavy cap (at most one criterion at Hand-wavy) before conclusions are
607	presented. If either condition is not met, revise the relevant sections and re-score — bounded
608	to **at most one re-perception pass** per analysis, per the rule stated in full under "How to
609	Apply This Gate" at the top of this document. If a criterion still fails after that single
610	pass, present it as an unresolved gap with a stated confidence caveat instead of re-scoring
611	again. This closing note restates that bound; it does not create a second, looser one.

## Solar Salt and Molten Nitrate Salt

Molten salts have been widely used as thermal energy storage and heat transfer fluid in solar power generation systems due to their wide working temperature, lower vapor pressure, moderate heat capacity, and good thermal stability. The salt mixture of 60 wt. % sodium nitrate and 40 wt. % potassium nitrate has been used successfully as a thermal energy storage medium in solar two central receiver projects and the commercial plant of Gemasolar in Spain.

## Two-Tank CSP Systems with Specific Temperatures

Gemasolar in Spain operates with a cold tank at 290°C and a hot tank at 585°C. The molten-salt storage technology at Crescent Dunes consists of a reservoir of 25,000 metric tonnes of potassium and sodium nitrate previously heated to 288°C.

## Crescent Dunes and Gemasolar Projects

Nitrate salt has been used in commercial solar parabolic trough and central receiver projects with two-tank (hot tank and cold tank) designs. Molten salt storage systems in the 565°C range can store green solar energy from thermal solar power stations, such as the Crescent Dunes solar plant in Nevada. Gemasolar is a commercial plant in Spain that has successfully used the sodium nitrate-potassium nitrate salt mixture as a thermal energy storage medium.

# Battery Storage Installation Costs (October 2025)

According to Ember's analysis, the total all-in capex for utility-scale BESS projects is broken down as follows:

**Total: $125/kWh**

The report states: "the total capex to build a large, long-duration utility-scale BESS project is around $125/kWh, comprising $75/kWh for the core equipment shipped from China and around $50/kWh for installation and grid connection."

**Equipment Costs: $75/kWh**
Core equipment—battery enclosures, Power Conversion Systems, and Energy Management Systems—costs approximately $75 per kilowatt-hour when sourced from Chinese manufacturers in markets with low import duties.

**Installation & Grid Connection: $50/kWh**
Engineering, procurement, construction services, and grid connection typically add roughly $50/kWh, though this figure varies significantly depending on grid connection fees, which can range from $30/kWh to $100/kWh in extreme cases.

This breakdown reflects real-world project pricing derived from recent auctions in Saudi Arabia, India, and Italy, combined with expert interviews conducted in October 2025.

input.command:
cat >> ".first-principles/analysis-20261010T150644Z.md" <<'FP_EOF'
## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does a 290–565 °C molten-salt thermal energy storage tank, charged and discharged through electricity (electricity → heat → electricity), actually achieve a round-trip *electrical* efficiency above 85%, and is a 5 MWh system of this type cost-competitive with a 5 MWh lithium-ion battery — or does the claim conflate a real thermal-storage-retention figure with a different, much lower, electricity-to-electricity figure?

**Success criteria:**
1. A Carnot-bound calculation for the heat-engine discharge step (565 °C hot side, ambient heat-rejection cold side) is computed and compared numerically against the claimed 85% figure.
2. Real deployed/specified thermal-electric ("Carnot battery"/ETES) systems are cited with their own electricity-to-electricity round-trip figures, compared against the 85% claim.
3. The specific equivocation between "thermal round-trip efficiency" (heat retained as heat) and "electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency" is named, with both figures reported side by side from the same sources where available.
4. An illustrative $/kWh cost comparison between a 5 MWh molten-salt TES + power-block system and a 5 MWh Li-ion BESS is produced, naming the scale-dependent cost driver (power-block minimum economic size) that the claim's "same nameplate capacity" framing elides.
5. A single verdict — true / false / true-with-major-caveats — is issued for the compound claim, with corrected figures for both the efficiency and cost sub-claims.
FP_EOF
echo done

4. Power-block capital cost at 5 MWh/~1 MW scale must be comparable to Li-ion's $/kWh — tested in C4: **fails** (several-fold gap).
5. The cited 85% figure, if literature-sourced, must refer to electricity-to-electricity and not heat-to-heat storage retention — tested in C3: **fails** (it is the heat-to-heat figure).

input.command:
cat > ".first-principles/analysis-20261010T150644Z.md.s3" <<'FP_EOF'
## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** The Carnot efficiency of a heat engine is η = 1 − Tc/Th (absolute temperatures). For Th = 565 °C = 838.15 K and Tc = 25 °C = 298.15 K (ambient heat-rejection), η = 1 − 298.15/838.15 = **0.644 (64.4%)**. For Tc = 40 °C = 313.15 K (typical air-cooled condenser), η = 1 − 313.15/838.15 = **0.626 (62.6%)**. This is the absolute theoretical ceiling for *any* heat engine — reversible or not — converting heat at 565 °C to work, rejecting to ambient; no real engine can exceed it. — source: Second Law of Thermodynamics / Carnot's theorem (standard thermodynamic relation); read-at-source: derivation shown above, a direct application of a textbook physical law, not a reported figure.
- **GT-2** Siemens Gamesa's Electric Thermal Energy Storage (ETES) pilot (Hamburg-Altenwerder): a resistance heater and blower charge ~1,000 t of volcanic rock to 650 °C; a steam turbine discharges it back to electricity. Stated performance: "up to 45 percent at full electric cycle" (electricity-to-electricity round trip) while "efficiency can be maintained at 98 percent while storing heat" (thermal retention only, not reconverted to electricity). — source: ASME, "Heated Volcanic Rocks Store Energy" (asme.org); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-3** Malta Inc.'s M100-10 Pumped Heat Energy Storage (PHES) system: electricity drives a heat pump that charges hot molten salt and a separate chilled-liquid cold store; a heat engine reconverts the stored temperature difference to electricity. Spec-sheet row "Overall System Efficiency AC to AC (RTEAC)," defined as "total roundtrip efficiency of the plant defined as the ratio of the delivered discharge energy to the delivered charge energy at the output terminals (parasitic included)": **53%–65%**, stated as "expected between 1st and Nth plant." — source: Malta M100 System Technical Specifications (maltainc.com / my.atainsights.com PDF); read-at-source: page 2, "Key Technical Specification for the Malta M100-10 Plant" table.
- **GT-4?** Highview Power's liquid air energy storage (LAES) is reported with a standalone round-trip efficiency of roughly 50–60% (rising to 50–90% only when paired with an external heat/cold source such as a gas turbine). Stiesdal's GridScale (basalt-rock storage) is reported with a round-trip efficiency of roughly 35–60%, rising toward 60% only when byproduct heat and cold are separately recovered and used (not reconverted to electricity). — cited to: power-technology.com, pv-magazine.com, scitechdaily.com summaries of each company's own disclosures; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary, cited sources not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-5** The U.S. DOE Solar Energy Technologies Program's year-2020 goal for molten-salt thermal energy storage: round-trip efficiency "greater than 93%," with a recommended two-tank "direct" system (Case 5) "estimated at >97%" — explicitly a thermal (kWh-th) metric, i.e., heat retained as heat, not electricity recovered. Paired cost target: "less than $15/kWh-th." — source: U.S. DOE / OSTI document (osti.gov/biblio/1111584); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full, including the document's own clarification that these are heat-to-heat (kWh-th) metrics.
- **GT-6** Concentrated-solar-power (CSP) industry literature assumption, used to size molten-salt energy density: "a round-trip efficiency of 95% for the storage" (thermal, heat-to-heat) combined with "a thermal-to-electric energy conversion of 40%" (the power block) — together implying roughly 38% stored-heat-to-delivered-electricity for the combined storage-plus-power-block system, exclusive of the charging step. — source: Reuters Events, "Understanding the energy density of thermal storage"; read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-7** Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project (Nevada): two-tank nitrate "solar salt" storage with a cold-tank base temperature of 280 °C and a hot-tank temperature of "almost 600 °C." This is the real, commercially-deployed operating range for two-tank nitrate solar-salt CSP storage, closely matching the claim's stated 290–565 °C. — source: Wikipedia, "Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project," Technology section; read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-8** As of October 2025, the all-in installed capex for a large, long-duration utility-scale lithium-ion BESS project is approximately **$125/kWh**, comprising ~$75/kWh for core equipment (battery enclosures, power-conversion system, energy-management system, sourced from China) and ~$50/kWh for installation, engineering/procurement/construction and grid connection; this reflects real auction and project pricing (Saudi Arabia, India, Italy) and October 2025 expert interviews. — source: Ember Energy, "How cheap is battery storage?" (ember-energy.org); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.

## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Treating the 290 °C cold tank as the Carnot cold reservoir

**What was tried:** An initial pass computed the Carnot ceiling using Tc = 290 °C (563.15 K) instead of ambient, on the reasoning that the claim states a 290–565 °C *range*, giving η = 1 − 563.15/838.15 ≈ 32.8% — a far more severe-looking refutation than the ~62–64% figure actually used in C1.

**Why abandoned:** This conflates the heat-transfer-fluid's return temperature inside the storage loop with the thermodynamic cycle's actual heat-rejection temperature. A Rankine power block's condenser rejects heat near ambient (25–40 °C), not at 290 °C; the 290 °C "cold tank" is simply the salt's return temperature after giving up heat to the steam generator, not where the cycle discharges to the environment. Using 290 °C as Tc is a plausible-looking but physically incorrect simplification (A-7, discarded as a candidate reading, promoted instead to a tested and accepted assumption in C1).

**What it ruled out:** This saves a future reviewer from re-deriving an overly pessimistic (and physically wrong) ceiling; it also shows that getting the physics right does not rescue the claim — even the more generous, correct ~62–64% ceiling is far short of 85%.

### Dead End: Reading the claim's architecture as a Malta-style heat-pump/cold-store Carnot battery

**What was tried:** Because the claim mentions "electric resistance heating *or heat pump*," an alternate reading treated the system as architecturally identical to Malta's reversible heat-pump/heat-engine cycle, which is not bounded by the simple single-engine Carnot ceiling C1 derives (a reversible heat-pump-charge + heat-engine-discharge cycle between a hot store and the ambient environment can in principle approach 100% round trip).

**Why abandoned:** The claim's stated temperature pair — both tanks above ambient (290 °C and 565 °C), with no sub-ambient cold store mentioned — matches the conventional two-tank "solar salt" CSP configuration (GT-7), not Malta's architecture, which pairs a hot molten-salt store with a separate chilled-liquid cold store below ambient. Pursuing this reading as the *primary* one would have been reasoning from the claim's wording in isolation rather than from what the stated temperatures actually describe (A-2).

**What it ruled out:** This reading was not discarded outright — it is addressed on its own terms in C2 using Malta's real commercial specification (GT-3), which shows that even the thermodynamically more favorable architecture tops out at 65%, not 85%. The dead end is recorded to show the more charitable reading was tested, not ignored.

### Dead End: Using Highview LAES and Stiesdal GridScale as the primary empirical anchors

**What was tried:** Highview Power's liquid air energy storage and Stiesdal's GridScale (basalt-rock storage) were initially considered as the leading real-world comparators for the claim's round-trip efficiency, since both are well-known "thermal/mechanical battery" technologies with published efficiency ranges (GT-4?).

**Why abandoned:** GT-4? is reported-by-delegate — the cited sources were not opened by this analysis, and neither technology's storage medium (cryogenic liquid air; basalt rock) is as close an architectural analog to electrically-charged molten salt as Siemens Gamesa's resistively-charged rock ETES or Malta's molten-salt-based PHES, both of which were read at source (GT-2, GT-3).

**What it ruled out:** GT-4? is retained only as directional corroboration (both report RTE well below 85%) rather than as load-bearing evidence for C1–C3, avoiding a HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on an unread citation.
FP_EOF

## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated and replace it with corrected figures: the achievable electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency for a 290–565 °C, electrically-charged, two-tank molten-salt system is on the order of 35–45% for the resistive-heating architecture the temperatures describe (chain C1), or at best 53–65% for the most favorable real alternative architecture found, a heat-pump-charged "Carnot battery" (chain C2) — never 85%, which exceeds even the idealized, lossless physical ceiling for the resistive case (chain C1). At 5 MWh, molten-salt TES is not cost-competitive with lithium-ion BESS; it is roughly 4–10x more expensive per kWh of nameplate capacity, dominated by the power block's lack of small-scale economies (chain C4), and loses a weighted multi-criteria comparison on capex, efficiency, power density and scale fit despite leading on cycle life and material risk (chain C6).

**Key insight:** The claim's 85% figure is not simply optimistic engineering — it is a real, correctly-sourced number describing a different physical quantity than the one asserted. Every literature source that reports ≥85% (DOE's >93% target, a 2-tank "direct" system's >97%, a vendor's own 98%) is measuring heat retained as heat inside the storage tank, not electricity recovered after reconversion through a heat engine; the same hardware's electricity-to-electricity figure is 40–53 percentage points lower in every case that states both numbers side by side (chain C3). This is a unit/scope equivocation, not a rounding error or an aggressive-but-plausible engineering estimate.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This is not a blanket dismissal of molten-salt thermal storage. At full commercial CSP scale — hundreds to thousands of MWh-thermal, charged by collected solar heat rather than purchased electricity — the technology is real, deployed, and economically sound on its own terms, because the power block's fixed cost is amortized over far more energy and the electricity round-trip metric this analysis evaluates does not apply to solar-heat charging (chain C5). The claim as written describes neither that scale nor that charging mode, so this caveat qualifies the technology's standing in general, not the verdict on the specific 5 MWh, electrically-charged claim (chain C5).

**Pre-check:** head C1 (HIGH), C2 (HIGH), C3 (HIGH), C4 (MEDIUM), C5 (MEDIUM), C6 (MEDIUM) · ?-marked: none directly · lowest cited: MEDIUM · Inputs ceiling: MEDIUM
**Confidence:** MEDIUM — the thermodynamic falsification (C1, C2, C3) is independently HIGH confidence and would stand even if the cost analysis were set aside entirely; the overall rating is capped by the cost and trade-off chains (C4, C5, C6), each MEDIUM because they rest on GT-11? (small-scale power-block capex, Phase 3 read failed: HTTP 403) and GT-10?/GT-9? (lithium-ion RTE and cycle life, reported-by-delegate, not opened), and on an assumed representative power rating (A-9) and assumed criteria weights (A-12). Each of these would be resolved by: accessing the ORC techno-economic review through a different channel or an actual EPC quote (GT-11?); reading a DOE/NREL storage-technology comparison directly (GT-9?, GT-10?). The sensitivity checks run in C4 and C6 (alternate power ratings, flip-test reweighting) show the *direction* of the cost and trade-off verdicts is robust even though the exact magnitude is not HIGH-confidence.

**Verdict: the compound claim is false as stated.** The efficiency sub-claim (>85% electricity-to-electricity round trip) is false and, for the architecture the stated temperatures describe, physically impossible; the cost-competitiveness sub-claim is false at the stated 5 MWh scale. Corrected figures: round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency ≈ 35–45% (resistive architecture) to at best 53–65% (best real heat-pump architecture found); installed cost ≈ $540–1,200/kWh for molten-salt TES + power block at 5 MWh versus ≈ $125/kWh for lithium-ion BESS at comparable scale.

134	## 5. Abandoned Reasoning
135	
136	### Dead End: Treating the 290 °C cold tank as the Carnot cold reservoir
137	
138	**What was tried:** An initial pass computed the Carnot ceiling using Tc = 290 °C (563.15 K) instead of ambient, on the reasoning that the claim states a 290–565 °C *range*, giving η = 1 − 563.15/838.15 ≈ 32.8% — a far more severe-looking refutation than the ~62–64% figure actually used in C1.
139	
140	**Why abandoned:** This conflates the heat-transfer-fluid's return temperature inside the storage loop with the thermodynamic cycle's actual heat-rejection temperature. A Rankine power block's condenser rejects heat near ambient (25–40 °C), not at 290 °C; the 290 °C "cold tank" is simply the salt's return temperature after giving up heat to the steam generator, not where the cycle discharges to the environment. Using 290 °C as Tc is a plausible-looking but physically incorrect simplification (A-7, discarded as a candidate reading, promoted instead to a tested and accepted assumption in C1).
141	
142	**What it ruled out:** This saves a future reviewer from re-deriving an overly pessimistic (and physically wrong) ceiling; it also shows that getting the physics right does not rescue the claim — even the more generous, correct ~62–64% ceiling is far short of 85%.
143	
144	### Dead End: Reading the claim's architecture as a Malta-style heat-pump/cold-store Carnot battery
145	
146	**What was tried:** Because the claim mentions "electric resistance heating *or heat pump*," an alternate reading treated the system as architecturally identical to Malta's reversible heat-pump/heat-engine cycle, which is not bounded by the simple single-engine Carnot ceiling C1 derives (a reversible heat-pump-charge + heat-engine-discharge cycle between a hot store and the ambient environment can in principle approach 100% round trip).
147	
148	**Why abandoned:** The claim's stated temperature pair — both tanks above ambient (290 °C and 565 °C), with no sub-ambient cold store mentioned — matches the conventional two-tank "solar salt" CSP configuration (GT-7), not Malta's architecture, which pairs a hot molten-salt store with a separate chilled-liquid cold store below ambient. Pursuing this reading as the *primary* one would have been reasoning from the claim's wording in isolation rather than from what the stated temperatures actually describe (A-2).
149	
150	**What it ruled out:** This reading was not discarded outright — it is addressed on its own terms in C2 using Malta's real commercial specification (GT-3), which shows that even the thermodynamically more favorable architecture tops out at 65%, not 85%. The dead end is recorded to show the more charitable reading was tested, not ignored.
151	
152	### Dead End: Using Highview LAES and Stiesdal GridScale as the primary empirical anchors
153	
154	**What was tried:** Highview Power's liquid air energy storage and Stiesdal's GridScale (basalt-rock storage) were initially considered as the leading real-world comparators for the claim's round-trip efficiency, since both are well-known "thermal/mechanical battery" technologies with published efficiency ranges (GT-4?).
155	
156	**Why abandoned:** GT-4? is reported-by-delegate — the cited sources were not opened by this analysis, and neither technology's storage medium (cryogenic liquid air; basalt rock) is as close an architectural analog to electrically-charged molten salt as Siemens Gamesa's resistively-charged rock ETES or Malta's molten-salt-based PHES, both of which were read at source (GT-2, GT-3).
157	
158	**What it ruled out:** GT-4? is retained only as directional corroboration (both report RTE well below 85%) rather than as load-bearing evidence for C1–C3, avoiding a HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on an unread citation.
159	## 6. Conclusion
160	
161	**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated and replace it with corrected figures: the achievable electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency for a 290–565 °C, electrically-charged, two-tank molten-salt system is on the order of 35–45% for the resistive-heating architecture the temperatures describe (chain C1), or at best 53–65% for the most favorable real alternative architecture found, a heat-pump-charged "Carnot battery" (chain C2) — never 85%, which exceeds even the idealized, lossless physical ceiling for the resistive case (chain C1). At 5 MWh, molten-salt TES is not cost-competitive with lithium-ion BESS; it is roughly 4–10x more expensive per kWh of nameplate capacity, dominated by the power block's lack of small-scale economies (chain C4), and loses a weighted multi-criteria comparison on capex, efficiency, power density and scale fit despite leading on cycle life and material risk (chain C6).
162	
163	**Key insight:** The claim's 85% figure is not simply optimistic engineering — it is a real, correctly-sourced number describing a different physical quantity than the one asserted. Every literature source that reports ≥85% (DOE's >93% target, a 2-tank "direct" system's >97%, a vendor's own 98%) is measuring heat retained as heat inside the storage tank, not electricity recovered after reconversion through a heat engine; the same hardware's electricity-to-electricity figure is 40–53 percentage points lower in every case that states both numbers side by side (chain C3). This is a unit/scope equivocation, not a rounding error or an aggressive-but-plausible engineering estimate.
164	
165	**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This is not a blanket dismissal of molten-salt thermal storage. At full commercial CSP scale — hundreds to thousands of MWh-thermal, charged by collected solar heat rather than purchased electricity — the technology is real, deployed, and economically sound on its own terms, because the power block's fixed cost is amortized over far more energy and the electricity round-trip metric this analysis evaluates does not apply to solar-heat charging (chain C5). The claim as written describes neither that scale nor that charging mode, so this caveat qualifies the technology's standing in general, not the verdict on the specific 5 MWh, electrically-charged claim (chain C5).

## Answer

**Recommendation:** The claim is false as stated. A 290–565 °C molten-salt system charged and discharged through electricity achieves roughly 35–45% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency (resistive architecture, chain C1), or at best 53–65% with the best real heat-pump-based architecture found (chain C2) — never 85%, which exceeds even the lossless Carnot ceiling for the resistive case (chain C1). At 5 MWh it is not cost-competitive with lithium-ion BESS, running roughly 4–10x more expensive per kWh (chain C4) and losing a weighted multi-criteria comparison (chain C6).

**Band (from §6):** MEDIUM — the thermodynamic falsification (chains C1, C2, C3) is independently HIGH confidence; the overall band is capped by the cost and trade-off chains (C4, C5, C6).

**Would change it:** A vendor-specified or independently measured system reporting ≥75% AC-to-AC round trip, or an actual EPC-quoted installed cost for a ~5 MWh/~1 MW molten-salt system within 2x of $125/kWh (chain C4) — the Phase 3 read of the small-scale power-block cost source (GT-11?) failed (HTTP 403) and is the most load-bearing unresolved input.
## 1. Problem Essence

**Core problem:** Does a 290–565 °C molten-salt thermal energy storage tank, charged and discharged through electricity (electricity → heat → electricity), actually achieve a round-trip *electrical* efficiency above 85%, and is a 5 MWh system of this type cost-competitive with a 5 MWh lithium-ion battery — or does the claim conflate a real thermal-storage-retention figure with a different, much lower, electricity-to-electricity figure?

**Success criteria:**
1. A Carnot-bound calculation for the heat-engine discharge step (565 °C hot side, ambient heat-rejection cold side) is computed and compared numerically against the claimed 85% figure.
2. Real deployed/specified thermal-electric ("Carnot battery"/ETES) systems are cited with their own electricity-to-electricity round-trip figures, compared against the 85% claim.
3. The specific equivocation between "thermal round-trip efficiency" (heat retained as heat) and "electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency" is named, with both figures reported side by side from the same sources where available.
4. An illustrative $/kWh cost comparison between a 5 MWh molten-salt TES + power-block system and a 5 MWh Li-ion BESS is produced, naming the scale-dependent cost driver (power-block minimum economic size) that the claim's "same nameplate capacity" framing elides.
5. A single verdict — true / false / true-with-major-caveats — is issued for the compound claim, with corrected figures for both the efficiency and cost sub-claims.
## 2. Assumptions Table

**Inversion check (companion technique — the claim is the "conclusion that feels too clean"):** inverted, the claim fails if *any* of its necessary preconditions is false. Five such preconditions were tested directly against evidence gathered below, independently of one another:

1. The Carnot ceiling at 565 °C/ambient must exceed 85% — tested in C1: **fails** (~62–64%).
2. A real deployed or vendor-specified system of this class must demonstrate ≥85% AC-to-AC round trip — tested in C2: **fails** (45–65% across the two plausible architectures).
3. The charging path must be a reversible heat-pump/cold-store cycle capable of exceeding the simple Carnot-engine ceiling — tested via the architecture read (A-2 below, supported by GT-7): the claim's 290–565 °C pairing (both tanks above ambient, no sub-ambient store mentioned) matches the simple resistive-heating convention, not a heat-pump Carnot battery, so this precondition **fails for the architecture the claim most plausibly describes**.
4. Power-block capital cost at 5 MWh/~1 MW scale must be comparable to Li-ion's $/kWh — tested in C4: **fails** (several-fold gap).
5. The cited 85% figure, if literature-sourced, must refer to electricity-to-electricity and not heat-to-heat storage retention — tested in C3: **fails** (it is the heat-to-heat figure).

All five independently-tested preconditions fail. This is a triangulated refutation rather than a single weak link, which is itself a finding the Self-Audit Gate's Sensitivity step will return to.

| Assumption | Type | Treatment | Verdict | Verification |
|------------|------|-----------|---------|---------------|
| A round-trip electricity-to-electricity efficiency above 85% is achievable for an electrically-charged molten-salt TES discharging through a heat engine between 565 °C and ambient. | untested belief | Verify via Carnot derivation (theoretical-limit) and real-world data | Discard — refuted independently by GT-1 (physical ceiling ~62–64%) and GT-2/GT-3 (best real systems 45–65%) | unverified — flagged, then discharged by GT-1/GT-2/GT-3 in chains C1–C2 |
| The claim's described architecture (290–565 °C, two-tank sensible-heat molten salt, "electric resistance heating or heat pump") is the simple resistive-heating + Rankine-discharge type, not a Malta-style reversible heat-pump/cold-store Carnot battery. | convention | Challenge before use | Accept — both tanks sit above ambient with no stated sub-ambient cold store; GT-7 shows this temperature pairing matches real two-tank "solar salt" CSP practice (resistive/direct-heat convention), not Malta's architecture | GT-7 (Crescent Dunes, Wikipedia, read-at-source) |
| A 5 MWh scale captures normal economies of scale for a molten-salt TES + power-block system. | untested belief | Verify against small-scale power-block cost data | Discard — GT-11? and general power-block engineering judgment; power blocks have a large minimum economic size that a 5 MWh system does not reach | unverified — flagged (GT-11? read attempt failed, Phase 3 failure recorded in §3) |
| "Nameplate capacity" (MWh) alone, with no stated power rating, is a sufficient basis to compare the two technologies' economics. | current constraint | Record what is missing; assume a representative power rating and flag the sensitivity | Accept — expires once the claim (or a reader) states an actual power/duration pairing; until then, 1 MW / 5-hour duration is used as an illustrative, explicitly flagged stand-in | unverified — flagged, sensitivity tested across 500 kW–2 MW in C4's confidence line |
| Round-trip efficiency is the dominant lever for levelized-cost-of-storage competitiveness at small scale, more than upfront capex. | convention | Challenge before use | Discard — at 5 MWh the capex gap (several-fold) dominates any plausible efficiency-driven revenue difference; see C4 | unverified — flagged, discharged by GT-8/GT-11? in chain C4 |
| Thermal losses over hold duration are a minor, scale-independent contributor to the claimed efficiency figure. | current constraint | Record expiry conditions | Accept with caveat — expires as tank size shrinks; a 5 MWh tank has a far less favorable surface-to-volume ratio than the multi-hundred-MWh tanks GT-5/GT-6's efficiency figures were measured on, so fractional losses are likely understated by those sources at this scale | unverified — flagged, not independently quantified in this analysis |
| The heat engine's relevant Carnot cold reservoir is the ambient heat-rejection (condenser) temperature, not the 290 °C cold-tank return temperature. | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate | Accept — a Rankine power block's heat-transfer-fluid return temperature (here, 290 °C) is not where the thermodynamic cycle rejects heat; the condenser does, near ambient | GT-1 (derivation); read-at-source (textbook thermodynamics) |
| Siemens Gamesa's rock-based ETES and Malta's molten-salt PHES are valid thermodynamic analogs for bounding the claim's achievable performance, despite differing storage media/temperatures. | untested belief | Verify via grounding in a named ground truth about each system, not bare analogy | Accept with caveat — both are sensible-heat storage with resistive-or-heat-pump charge and heat-engine discharge; Siemens Gamesa's higher hot-side temperature (650 °C vs. the claim's 565 °C) gives it a *higher* theoretical ceiling than the claim's system, so its 45% real-world figure understates, if anything, how far short of 85% the claim's actual (cooler) system would fall | GT-2, GT-3 (both read-at-source) |
| A representative power rating of 1 MW / 5-hour discharge duration is a reasonable basis for an illustrative $/kWh cost comparison at 5 MWh. | untested belief | Flag and bracket; test sensitivity across plausible alternatives | Accept with caveat, flagged | unverified — flagged; sensitivity checked at 500 kW/10h and 2 MW/2.5h in chain C4 |
| Resistive (Joule) electric heating converts electrical energy to heat at approximately 98–100% efficiency. | physical law | Accept as ground-truth candidate | Accept | read-at-source (standard electrical-engineering definition; minor transmission/distribution losses only) |
| At full commercial CSP scale, the thermal input to molten-salt storage is collected solar heat rather than purchased electricity, so electricity round-trip efficiency is not the primary economic metric for that use case. | current constraint | Record scope; not applicable to the claim's own framing (which specifies electric charging) | Accept, scoped to chain C5 only | GT-5, GT-7 (both read-at-source; context, not load-bearing for the claim as stated) |
| The six trade-off criteria and their relative weights (capex ×5, round-trip efficiency ×4, scale/duration fit ×4, power density/ramp rate ×3, cycle life ×2, material risk ×2) reflect genuine priorities for a standalone 5 MWh storage buyer, locked before scoring. | untested belief | Flag and test via flip-test sensitivity, per the trade-off procedure's discipline of locking weights before scoring | Accept with caveat — the flip test in C6 shows no single-criterion reweight changes the winner, so the ranking is robust to disagreement about the exact weights | unverified — flagged; flip-test sensitivity reported in chain C6 |
## 3. Ground Truths

- **GT-1** The Carnot efficiency of a heat engine is η = 1 − Tc/Th (absolute temperatures). For Th = 565 °C = 838.15 K and Tc = 25 °C = 298.15 K (ambient heat-rejection), η = 1 − 298.15/838.15 = **0.644 (64.4%)**. For Tc = 40 °C = 313.15 K (typical air-cooled condenser), η = 1 − 313.15/838.15 = **0.626 (62.6%)**. This is the absolute theoretical ceiling for *any* heat engine — reversible or not — converting heat at 565 °C to work, rejecting to ambient; no real engine can exceed it. — source: Second Law of Thermodynamics / Carnot's theorem (standard thermodynamic relation); read-at-source: derivation shown above, a direct application of a textbook physical law, not a reported figure.
- **GT-2** Siemens Gamesa's Electric Thermal Energy Storage (ETES) pilot (Hamburg-Altenwerder): a resistance heater and blower charge ~1,000 t of volcanic rock to 650 °C; a steam turbine discharges it back to electricity. Stated performance: "up to 45 percent at full electric cycle" (electricity-to-electricity round trip) while "efficiency can be maintained at 98 percent while storing heat" (thermal retention only, not reconverted to electricity). — source: ASME, "Heated Volcanic Rocks Store Energy" (asme.org); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-3** Malta Inc.'s M100-10 Pumped Heat Energy Storage (PHES) system: electricity drives a heat pump that charges hot molten salt and a separate chilled-liquid cold store; a heat engine reconverts the stored temperature difference to electricity. Spec-sheet row "Overall System Efficiency AC to AC (RTEAC)," defined as "total roundtrip efficiency of the plant defined as the ratio of the delivered discharge energy to the delivered charge energy at the output terminals (parasitic included)": **53%–65%**, stated as "expected between 1st and Nth plant." The same spec sheet gives "Charge Ramp Rate – Hot: 25%/min," "Discharge Ramp Rate – Hot: 25%/min," and "Start-up Time for 'Hot Start' – Discharging: 10 minutes" (minutes-scale response, not sub-second), and states the plant "requires well-understood and readily available raw materials and commodity products, including solar salt and antifreeze, rather than any rare earth materials or critical minerals in limited supply." — source: Malta M100 System Technical Specifications (maltainc.com / my.atainsights.com PDF); read-at-source: page 1 (materials statement) and page 2, "Key Technical Specification for the Malta M100-10 Plant" table (RTEAC and ramp-rate rows).
- **GT-4?** Highview Power's liquid air energy storage (LAES) is reported with a standalone round-trip efficiency of roughly 50–60% (rising to 50–90% only when paired with an external heat/cold source such as a gas turbine). Stiesdal's GridScale (basalt-rock storage) is reported with a round-trip efficiency of roughly 35–60%, rising toward 60% only when byproduct heat and cold are separately recovered and used (not reconverted to electricity). — cited to: power-technology.com, pv-magazine.com, scitechdaily.com summaries of each company's own disclosures; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary, cited sources not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-5** The U.S. DOE Solar Energy Technologies Program's year-2020 goal for molten-salt thermal energy storage: round-trip efficiency "greater than 93%," with a recommended two-tank "direct" system (Case 5) "estimated at >97%" — explicitly a thermal (kWh-th) metric, i.e., heat retained as heat, not electricity recovered. Paired cost target: "less than $15/kWh-th." — source: U.S. DOE / OSTI document (osti.gov/biblio/1111584); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full, including the document's own clarification that these are heat-to-heat (kWh-th) metrics.
- **GT-6** Concentrated-solar-power (CSP) industry literature assumption, used to size molten-salt energy density: "a round-trip efficiency of 95% for the storage" (thermal, heat-to-heat) combined with "a thermal-to-electric energy conversion of 40%" (the power block) — together implying roughly 38% stored-heat-to-delivered-electricity for the combined storage-plus-power-block system, exclusive of the charging step. — source: Reuters Events, "Understanding the energy density of thermal storage"; read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-7** Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project (Nevada): two-tank nitrate "solar salt" storage with a cold-tank base temperature of 280 °C and a hot-tank temperature of "almost 600 °C." This is the real, commercially-deployed operating range for two-tank nitrate solar-salt CSP storage, closely matching the claim's stated 290–565 °C. — source: Wikipedia, "Crescent Dunes Solar Energy Project," Technology section; read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-8** As of October 2025, the all-in installed capex for a large, long-duration utility-scale lithium-ion BESS project is approximately **$125/kWh**, comprising ~$75/kWh for core equipment (battery enclosures, power-conversion system, energy-management system, sourced from China) and ~$50/kWh for installation, engineering/procurement/construction and grid connection; this reflects real auction and project pricing (Saudi Arabia, India, Italy) and October 2025 expert interviews. — source: Ember Energy, "How cheap is battery storage?" (ember-energy.org); read-at-source: direct quotes above, fetched and read in full.
- **GT-9?** Lithium iron phosphate (LFP) cells used in stationary storage typically achieve 6,000–10,000 full cycles before capacity fades to 70–80% of nameplate, with a 15–20 year calendar life. — cited to: battery-degradation literature survey; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary, cited sources not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-10?** Utility-scale lithium-ion BESS AC-to-AC round-trip efficiency is typically in the 85–95% range. — cited to: general energy-storage technology comparisons; reported-by-delegate: WebSearch summary, specific source not opened by this analysis.
- **GT-11?** Small-scale (sub-1 MW to a few MW) steam/Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC) power-block capital cost is reported on the order of $2,000–3,500/kWe — substantially higher per kW than utility-scale (tens to hundreds of MW) steam-turbine power blocks, reflecting the lack of manufacturing-scale economies for turbine/generator/condenser/heat-exchanger equipment below a few MW. — cited to: "Small Scale Organic Rankine Cycle (ORC): A Techno-Economic Review" (MDPI Energies 10(4):413, doi:10.3390/en10040413); unverified: a Phase 3 read of this source was attempted (WebFetch on https://www.mdpi.com/1996-1073/10/4/413) and failed with **HTTP 403 Forbidden**; the figure is carried forward from a prior WebSearch summary only.

**Provenance summary:**

## 4. Derivation Chains

### Conclusion C1: An 85% electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency is thermodynamically impossible for the resistive-heating architecture the claim describes; the physical ceiling is ~62–64%

GT-1 (Carnot ceiling at 565°C/ambient, 62–64%) + GT-7 (290–565°C matches real two-tank solar-salt CSP practice, confirming the resistive-heating reading)
→ a resistive ("Joule") charge path converts electrical energy to heat at essentially 100% efficiency [Assumes: A-10], so for this architecture the round-trip ceiling is set almost entirely by the heat-engine discharge step
→ that discharge step's absolute physical ceiling is the Carnot efficiency between the 565°C salt temperature and the ambient heat-rejection temperature, 62–64%, not the 290°C cold-tank return temperature [Assumes: A-7]
→ the claimed 85% round-trip figure exceeds this reversible, lossless-engine ceiling by 20 or more percentage points, so it cannot be achieved by any heat engine operating between these two reservoirs, real or ideal
→[2nd] a developer or utility that accepted 85% at face value would underwrite a project whose modeled arbitrage revenue is roughly double what a corrected ~35–45% (C2) figure supports, and that shortfall surfaces the first time the plant is metered
→[3rd] repeated instances of this error across a market would attach a credibility discount to molten-salt TES generally, chilling investment in the large-scale CSP-integrated deployments (C5) where the technology's real advantages do not depend on beating lithium-ion's electrical round trip

*Second-order lenses applied: **actor lens** — the developer/utility that underwrites on the wrong figure, and the market that later discounts the technology's credibility; **time lens** — the shortfall surfaces immediately on first dispatch/metering, the reputational effect compounds over repeated deployments. ## 5. Abandoned Reasoning

### Dead End: Treating the 290 °C cold tank as the Carnot cold reservoir

**What was tried:** An initial pass computed the Carnot ceiling using Tc = 290 °C (563.15 K) instead of ambient, on the reasoning that the claim states a 290–565 °C *range*, giving η = 1 − 563.15/838.15 ≈ 32.8% — a far more severe-looking refutation than the ~62–64% figure actually used in C1.

**Why abandoned:** This conflates the heat-transfer-fluid's return temperature inside the storage loop with the thermodynamic cycle's actual heat-rejection temperature. A Rankine power block's condenser rejects heat near ambient (25–40 °C), not at 290 °C; the 290 °C "cold tank" is simply the salt's return temperature after giving up heat to the steam generator, not where the cycle discharges to the environment. Using 290 °C as Tc is a plausible-looking but physically incorrect simplification (A-7, discarded as a candidate reading, promoted instead to a tested and accepted assumption in C1).

**What it ruled out:** This saves a future reviewer from re-deriving an overly pessimistic (and physically wrong) ceiling; it also shows that getting the physics right does not rescue the claim — even the more generous, correct ~62–64% ceiling is far short of 85%.

### Dead End: Reading the claim's architecture as a Malta-style heat-pump/cold-store Carnot battery

**What was tried:** Because the claim mentions "electric resistance heating *or heat pump*," an alternate reading treated the system as architecturally identical to Malta's reversible heat-pump/heat-engine cycle, which is not bounded by the simple single-engine Carnot ceiling C1 derives (a reversible heat-pump-charge + heat-engine-discharge cycle between a hot store and the ambient environment can in principle approach 100% round trip).

**Why abandoned:** The claim's stated temperature pair — both tanks above ambient (290 °C and 565 °C), with no sub-ambient cold store mentioned — matches the conventional two-tank "solar salt" CSP configuration (GT-7), not Malta's architecture, which pairs a hot molten-salt store with a separate chilled-liquid cold store below ambient. Pursuing this reading as the *primary* one would have been reasoning from the claim's wording in isolation rather than from what the stated temperatures actually describe (A-2).

**What it ruled out:** This reading was not discarded outright — it is addressed on its own terms in C2 using Malta's real commercial specification (GT-3), which shows that even the thermodynamically more favorable architecture tops out at 65%, not 85%. The dead end is recorded to show the more charitable reading was tested, not ignored.

### Dead End: Using Highview LAES and Stiesdal GridScale as the primary empirical anchors

**What was tried:** Highview Power's liquid air energy storage and Stiesdal's GridScale (basalt-rock storage) were initially considered as the leading real-world comparators for the claim's round-trip efficiency, since both are well-known "thermal/mechanical battery" technologies with published efficiency ranges (GT-4?).

**Why abandoned:** GT-4? is reported-by-delegate — the cited sources were not opened by this analysis, and neither technology's storage medium (cryogenic liquid air; basalt rock) is as close an architectural analog to electrically-charged molten salt as Siemens Gamesa's resistively-charged rock ETES or Malta's molten-salt-based PHES, both of which were read at source (GT-2, GT-3).

**What it ruled out:** GT-4? is retained only as directional corroboration (both report RTE well below 85%) rather than as load-bearing evidence for C1–C3, avoiding a HIGH-confidence conclusion resting on an unread citation.
## 6. Conclusion

**Recommended approach:** Reject the claim as stated and replace it with corrected figures: the achievable electricity-to-electricity round-trip efficiency for a 290–565 °C, electrically-charged, two-tank molten-salt system is on the order of 35–45% for the resistive-heating architecture the temperatures describe (chain C1), or at best 53–65% for the most favorable real alternative architecture found, a heat-pump-charged "Carnot battery" (chain C2) — never 85%, which exceeds even the idealized, lossless physical ceiling for the resistive case (chain C1). At 5 MWh, molten-salt TES is not cost-competitive with lithium-ion BESS; it is roughly 4–10x more expensive per kWh of nameplate capacity, dominated by the power block's lack of small-scale economies (chain C4), and loses a weighted multi-criteria comparison on capex, efficiency, power density and scale fit despite leading on cycle life and material risk (chain C6).

**Key insight:** The claim's 85% figure is not simply optimistic engineering — it is a real, correctly-sourced number describing a different physical quantity than the one asserted. Every literature source that reports ≥85% (DOE's >93% target, a 2-tank "direct" system's >97%, a vendor's own 98%) is measuring heat retained as heat inside the storage tank, not electricity recovered after reconversion through a heat engine; the same hardware's electricity-to-electricity figure is 40–53 percentage points lower in every case that states both numbers side by side (chain C3). This is a unit/scope equivocation, not a rounding error or an aggressive-but-plausible engineering estimate.

**Trade-offs acknowledged:** This is not a blanket dismissal of molten-salt thermal storage. At full commercial CSP scale — hundreds to thousands of MWh-thermal, charged by collected solar heat rather than purchased electricity — the technology is real, deployed, and economically sound on its own terms, because the power block's fixed cost is amortized over far more energy and the electricity round-trip metric this analysis evaluates does not apply to solar-heat charging (chain C5). The claim as written describes neither that scale nor that charging mode, so this caveat qualifies the technology's standing in general, not the verdict on the specific 5 MWh, electrically-charged claim (chain C5).

## Verdict: False — on both the physics and the economics

**The 85% figure is thermodynamically impossible for the system as described.** At 565°C/ambient, the Carnot ceiling for converting heat back to electricity is **~62-64%** — a hard physical limit, not an engineering shortfall. No real engine can exceed it. The claimed 85% round-trip exceeds even a perfect, lossless heat engine by 20+ points.

**What's actually achievable:**
- Resistive-heating architecture (matches the stated 290–565°C range, which mirrors real two-tank "solar salt" CSP plants like Crescent Dunes): **~35–45%** electricity-to-electricity round trip. Siemens Gamesa's rock-based ETES pilot — at a *higher*, more favorable 650°C — only hits **45%**.
- Best-case alternative reading (a Malta-style reversible heat-pump "Carnot battery," not bounded by the single-engine ceiling): Malta's own commercial spec tops out at **53–65%** AC-to-AC.
- Nothing found anywhere approaches 85%.

**Where the 85%+ number actually comes from — the equivocation:** Every source reporting ≥85% (DOE's >93% target, a two-tank "direct" system's >97%, Siemens Gamesa's own 98%) is measuring **heat retained as heat** inside the tank, not electricity recovered after reconversion. Siemens Gamesa states both numbers for the *same hardware*: 98% thermal retention vs. 45% full electric cycle — a 53-point gap. The claim takes a correctly-sourced thermal-retention figure and relabels it as an electrical round-trip figure. That's the core error, not a rounding issue.

**Cost-competitiveness also fails, independently.** At 5 MWh, the power block (steam/ORC turbine) doesn't reach its economic minimum scale — bracketed installed cost comes to roughly **$540–1,200/kWh** versus lithium-ion's current **~$125/kWh** (2025 utility-scale pricing), a 4–10x gap. A weighted comparison across capex, efficiency, cycle life, ramp rate, and scale fit has lithium-ion winning 96 to 48, robust to reasonable reweighting. Molten salt only wins on cycle life (no electrochemical fade) and material-supply risk — both minor factors at this scale.

**Important caveat:** this doesn't indict molten-salt storage generally. At real CSP scale (hundreds–thousands of MWh-thermal, charged by collected solar heat, not purchased electricity), the economics work fine — because the power block's fixed cost amortizes over far more energy, and electrical round-trip efficiency isn't the relevant metric there. The claim just describes a scale and charging mode that doesn't match where this technology is actually viable.

**Confidence:** the thermodynamic refutation (Carnot ceiling + real-world precedent + the heat/electricity equivocation) is independently high-confidence — three separate lines of evidence, any one of which alone would sink the claim. The cost analysis is medium-confidence, limited by one unverified small-scale power-block cost source (a paywalled techno-economic review) and reported-but-unverified lithium-ion cycle-life/efficiency figures — though sensitivity checks show the cost gap's *direction* holds across a wide range of assumptions.

Full report with sourcing, derivation chains, and the adversarial self-check is saved at `.first-principles/report-20261010T150644Z.md` (and PDF) in the working directory, if you want the complete trace.
